q: In a perceptron, what happens to the weighted sum of the inputs before the activation function sees it?
options: It is squared to measure the error
It is divided by the number of inputs
It is compared with the true label
It has a bias added to it
explain: The perceptron sums the weighted inputs and then adds a bias. Comparing with a label happens in the cost function, outside the neuron.

q: A single perceptron fails to learn the XOR function however long it trains. Why?
options: XOR needs more input nodes than a perceptron allows
A step function cannot ever output the value 1
Random initialisation always starts it in the wrong place
The XOR classes cannot be separated by one straight line
explain: XOR cannot be split by one straight boundary, so a single weighted sum and activation cannot separate its classes. Training longer or starting from other random weights does not remove this limit.
flag: The slide only says a single perceptron learns linearly separable patterns. That XOR is not linearly separable is standard textbook knowledge.

q: How does mean squared error treat a prediction that is very far from its target compared with one that is close?
options: It treats both errors as the same size of mistake
It penalises the far prediction much more than the close one
It ignores any error above a fixed threshold
It rewards the far prediction so the model learns faster
explain: Squaring the distance makes far points cost much more than near points. Treating all sizes alike ignores the squaring.
flag: The slide says errors grow exponentially, which is more precisely quadratic growth, so the stem avoids that word.

q: At the current weight, the slope of the cost function is positive. What does this tell gradient descent?
options: Increase the weight, because a positive slope means it is too small
Stop, because a positive slope means the minimum has been reached
Reset the weight to a new random value
Decrease the weight, because moving against the slope lowers the cost
explain: Gradient descent moves in the negative direction of the derivative. With a positive slope that means decreasing the weight, and increasing it would raise the cost.

q: Describe how a single perceptron turns its inputs into an output.
model: Each input value is multiplied by the weight on its connection. The products are added together to give a weighted sum, and a bias is added to that sum. The result passes to an activation function, which decides whether the neuron fires. With a step function the output is one of two values. The weights and bias start random and are adjusted during training so that the error of the output becomes smaller.
points: Inputs are multiplied by their weights and summed
A bias is added to the sum
An activation function decides whether the neuron fires
Weights and bias are learned to reduce the output error

q: Explain the purpose of an activation function and give one example.
model: An activation function looks at the weighted sum produced by a neuron and decides whether the output connections should fire. The step function is the simplest example, giving one of two values depending on the sum. Sigmoid and softmax are other examples and are often used so that the output of a classification network is a probability. The choice of activation function depends on the task the network has to do.
points: It checks the weighted sum of a neuron
It decides whether the output connections fire
A step function is a valid example
Sigmoid or softmax is a valid example

q: Explain why a single perceptron is limited and how a network of perceptrons goes further.
model: A single perceptron can only learn patterns that are linearly separable, so it cannot solve a problem where one straight boundary cannot split the classes. XOR is a standard example. Placing thousands of perceptrons in consecutive layers lets them work together. Each layer passes its results on, and the network turns the input data into predictions based on the presence or absence of features.
points: A single perceptron only learns linearly separable patterns
Names a problem it cannot learn, such as XOR
A network uses many perceptrons in consecutive layers
Layers turn inputs into predictions based on features
flag: The slides only say a network turns inputs into predictions based on features. The claim that layers overcome the linear limit is standard textbook knowledge.

q: Explain how an artificial neural network works and how learning takes place during training. Discuss trainable parameters, particularly weights and biases, and their roles in determining the output.
model: An artificial neural network is made of layers of neurons: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up with a bias and passes the result through an activation function. The outputs flow forward layer by layer to give a prediction. Training compares the prediction with the true value using a loss function. The error is sent back through the network and the weights and biases are adjusted by backpropagation and gradient descent to reduce it, and this repeats over many examples. Weights and biases are the trainable parameters. A weight sets how strongly an input affects a neuron. A bias shifts the weighted sum so the neuron can activate even when its inputs are zero.
points: Layers of neurons, input, hidden and output
Each neuron takes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation function
Training compares predictions with targets using a loss
Weights and biases are adjusted to reduce the loss
Weights set input strength, bias shifts the sum

q: Which quantities are typically adjusted during training of a feedforward neural network?
options: Input features and target labels
Weights and biases
Activation function names and dataset size
Number of training observations and output classes
explain: Weights and biases are the trainable parameters. The data and the architecture stay fixed during training.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 10

q: What is the main consequence of using only linear activation functions throughout a multilayer feedforward network?
options: The network would automatically become a recurrent model
The network would be unable to represent nonlinear mappings through its stacked layers
The network would no longer require trainable weights
The network would always produce binary outputs
explain: A stack of linear layers collapses into one linear function, so the extra layers add no power to model nonlinear patterns.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 11
flag: That stacked linear layers collapse into one linear function is standard textbook reasoning.
